name: Lower face rejuvenation filler (jowl filler)

lead: Jowl filler uses injectable dermal filler, most often hyaluronic acid, to fill the hollow in front of the jowl and the marionette area so the jaw line looks smoother and more continuous.

The filler adds volume under the skin, and the result is visible right after injection. Hyaluronic acid products are usually cross-linked for stability. It is a mainstream aesthetic procedure, while trials focused on jowls are few and small; one registered trial of fillers for jowl improvement enrolled 16 participants.

paras: It is a clinic treatment done with injections in a short visit, with results seen immediately and settling over following days. Many people combine it with other lower-face treatments.
Bruising, redness and pain are common. Rare vascular complications can cause skin necrosis or permanent vision loss. Fillers are regulated as medical devices.

angle.text: A smoother lower face and a cleaner jaw line. Filler along the pre-jowl and marionette areas restores lost volume and softens jowls, with the result visible right after injection. Jowl-specific trial data is small.

lead: Jowl filler refers to injecting dermal filler into the pre-jowl, marionette and lower-face areas to restore lost volume and smooth the line of the jaw.

Dermal fillers are substances injected into connective tissue; hyaluronic acid is the most common material, and fillers are used for wrinkles, volume loss and enhancement of the lips, cheeks and jawline [1]. Common side effects include bruising, redness and pain; rare vascular complications can cause permanent vision loss or skin necrosis [1].
Clinical research specific to jowls is small: one registered trial of fillers for jowl improvement enrolled 16 participants [2].

paras: Fillers are used to correct folds, restore volume lost with age and contour areas such as the jawline [1]. Filler materials include hyaluronic acid, poly-L-lactic acid, PMMA, collagen and autologous fat [1].

Reported adverse effects include bruising, redness, itching, infection, allergic reaction, lumps and scarring. Retrograde embolisation into eye arteries can cause blindness, and delayed skin necrosis can follow vascular events [1]. In the US fillers are regulated as medical devices and must be prescribed and administered by a provider; in the EU and UK they are CE-marked devices [1].

A registered clinical study, "Jowl Improvement With Injectable Fillers", was completed in 2020 with 16 participants [2]. A phase 3 trial of an injectable material for wrinkle correction listing jowls was registered in 2007 and withdrawn [3]. No results are summarised here.
